sources.title: Ayodeji Olukoju: Lagos in the 19th Century, 2019
sources.note: Author-posted Oxford Research Encyclopedia abstract checked. DOI 10.1093/acrefore/9780190277734.013.281. British annexation 1861, produce exports, returnee communities and professional education; full encyclopedia entry inaccessible.

sources.title: Ayodeji Ogunnaike: The Transcontinental Genealogy of the Afro-Brazilian Mosque, 2022
sources.note: Direct Yale MAVCOR research article. Sections on Shitta Bey Mosque and spread of Afro-Brazilian architecture: 1894 mosque, house plans, Ebun House about 1913 and cap-losing nickname. No universal housing claim; nickname paraphrased, not invented.

sources.title: Adewumi Damilola Adebayo: Electricity, Agency and Class in Lagos Colony, 2023/2024
sources.note: Complete open-access article text directly read; DOI 10.1093/pastj/gtad001. Online April 2023, Past & Present 262 (2024), 168 to 206. School science, 1865 experiments, 1895 tax resistance and electric lighting from 1898. Publisher direct fetch failed.

sources.title: Ayodeji Olukoju: Infrastructure Development and Urban Facilities in Lagos, 1861 to 2000, 2003
sources.note: Direct complete IFRA research book. Chapter 3 paragraphs 1 to 5: wells, cesspools, 1882 proposals and Iju commissioning 1 July 1915. Paragraphs use archival correspondence and contemporary newspapers. Later commissioning explicitly beyond map interval.

sources.title: Nozomi Sawada: A Re-examination of Pioneering Newspaper Enterprises, 2015
sources.note: Direct university-hosted original archival research, printed 45 and 53. Iwe Irohin Eko title and translation printed together on 45; 1888 publication, price and bilingual format on 53. Bibliography lists consulted 9 May 1891 issue. The writing sample preserves the article’s unaccented historical title transcription, without claiming facsimile inspection.

sources.title: Participation and Law’s Authority: Nigeria’s legal history, 2023
sources.note: Publisher full indexed section II checked, citing the 28 February 1906 Letters Patent and the subsequent 1913 boundary order/1914 legal amalgamation. Used for institutional changes, not the article’s broader legal-philosophical argument.

sources.title: The National Archives: Colonial administration records, Nigeria
sources.note: Official archive guide: Lagos colony in the 1860s, Northern/Southern Nigeria amalgamation 1914, independence 1960.

sources.title: Michael Lobban: Removing Rulers in the Niger Delta, 1887 to 1897, 2021
sources.note: Direct complete open-access chapter in Imperial Incarceration, especially Jaja of Opobo section. Archival research on treaty rights, detention, inquiry and exile. Public copy distinguishes removal in 1887 from the imported 1914 endpoint.

sources.title: Michael Ehis Odijie and Uzoamaka Nwachukwu: Colonial-Imposed Slavery and African Abolitionism, 2024/2025
sources.note: Original Slavery & Abolition research, DOI 10.1080/0144039X.2024.2353095. Full indexed article passages checked via PMC and publisher results; direct PMC fetch challenged. House organization, Jaja’s social mobility and the 1901 Native House Rule Ordinance, contested by Lagos abolitionists.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Boys paddling Sam Yubis’s canoe, Opobo, Nigeria
sources.note: Official indexed catalog checked; image itself not inspected. Eliot Elisofon Photographic Archives EEPA 1995-170078, albumen photograph dated 1877 to 1895, described as about thirty boys paddling. The historical caption does not establish ages or legal status.

sources.title: Chambers’s Journal: “Chop” with King Ja-Ja, 10 July 1886
sources.note: Direct complete primary travel account, printed 433 to 436. Anonymous colonial visitor’s narrow material observations only: nail-making forge, palace on piles, Accra craftspeople and royal banquet. Racist generalizations and purported medical explanations excluded. Observations are explicitly attributed, not universal customs.

sources.title: University of Hildesheim: Jaja’s letter to Lord Salisbury, 26 March 1886
sources.note: Direct Harald Kleinschmidt teaching collection of historical documents, printed and human PDF page 108, section 9.7.1.2. Transcribes the English letter and cites TNA FO 84/1762 No. 1, via S. J. S. Cookey, King Jaja of the Niger Delta, page 120. Nine-word sample preserved exactly; no autograph or Ibani text claimed.

sources.title: Jane I. Guyer: Manillas, Money and the Cost of Legitimacy in the mid-20th Century
sources.note: Complete text mirror of original British Museum Money in Africa research chapter, printed 38 to 44, directly read. Royal account book dated 1944 to 1954, chiefly 1944 to 1948; Stephen Ugborgu Jaja III was deposed in 1949, so later documents express contested authority. Used for specific account entries and continuing institutions, not a neutral census or proof of uninterrupted rule.

sources.title: Berihun Kassa Hailu and Jemal Abebe Jemere: Recalling the History of Sultan Mohammed Hanfare, 2017
sources.note: Direct research article based on secondary histories and oral interviews, African Journal of History and Culture 9(9), 72 to 77. Used narrowly for capital shift, Aydahiso/Mudaito dynasty and disputed succession. Its description of a nineteenth-century ruler as democratic is not adopted. Chronology differs from Ashami’s sketch, explicitly acknowledged in public copy.

sources.title: Max Planck Institute: In Pursuit of Afar Nomads, edited field notes and historical sketch, 2018
sources.note: Direct complete institutional publication of Glynn Flood’s 1973 to 1975 records, edited by Maknun Ashami, Jean Lydall and Michèle Flood. Ashami’s historical sketch printed 10 to 19 supplies canal settlement, malak functions, 1964 schooling and 1975 rupture. Do not use internally inconsistent founding dates: printed 10 gives mid-seventeenth century, printed 12 gives 1557, while Hailu/Jemere date dynasty to 1734.

sources.title: Tom Lavers: Modernization, State-Building, and the Hydraulic Mission in Imperial and Revolutionary Ethiopia, 2024
sources.note: Direct full Oxford University Press chapter in Dams, Power, and the Politics of Ethiopia’s Renaissance. Awash discussion: centuries of irrigation, 1895 defeat without direct administration, 1960s Tendaho negotiations and cotton expansion, unequal effects on pastoralists. Public copy uses modern episodes as dated continuation.

sources.title: Bisrat Teklesilassie Yazew: Women’s Contributions versus Men’s Patriarchal Status among Afar Pastoralists, 2024
sources.note: Original qualitative study in Heliyon 10(14), e34469. Full indexed methodology and results checked; direct PMC fetch challenged. Interviews, observations and focus groups in Lower Awash communities including Asaita, Afambo, Dubti and Mille. Specific market, water, house-moving and mutual support observations used as 2024 research, not projected into the seventeenth century.

sources.title: Richard J. Hayward: Qafar (East Cushitic), The Handbook of Morphology
sources.note: Direct publisher PDF, printed 629 / human PDF page 6, example (4): áh roóbu, This is rain. Handbook first published 1998; 2001 edition cited in Oxford Handbook of Ethiopian Languages bibliography. Hayward’s note 1 calls this a linguistic transcription, differing from standard Qafar orthography; acute accent denotes high tone. PDF text witness checked, screenshot rendering unavailable.

proposedOverrides.summary: A lower Awash political centre sustained by irrigation, herding and Afar institutions.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Outline broadly covers Lagos/coastal hinterland; no independent kingdom claimed after 1861. Colonial administration changed in 1886, 1906 and 1914. Historical Yoruba newspaper title is an attested scholarly transcription. Iju commissioning 1915 explicitly follows map window.

Niger Delta location fits Opobo and hinterland. Window includes both independent/protectorate treaty phase and colonial rule after Jaja’s 1887 removal. No 1914 destruction claimed. 1940s accounts are explicitly later continuation. Writing is an 1886 English diplomatic transcription, not an invented Ibani sample.

Imported outline spans much wider Afar territory than core Awsa delta. No claim of uniform sovereignty or equivalence with all Afar. Imamate and later Mudaito/Aydahiso sultanate distinguished. Sources disagree over rise of dynasty; 1734 is identified as one chronology, not falsely unanimous. Neither 1815 nor 1895 is treated as final disappearance. Later evidence dates are explicit. Original sample is modern linguistic transcription, not standard orthography or early manuscript.
